title: Part 2, Chapter 36
paragraphs: Which relates the strange and unimaginable adventure of the Distressed Duenna, also known as the Countess Trifaldi, along with a letter that Sancho Panza wrote to his wife, Teresa Panza

The duke had a majordomo with a playful, mischievous streak. It was he who had played Merlin, organized every detail of the recent adventure, written the verses, and arranged for a page to act the part of Dulcinea; and now, with the help of his master and mistress, he put together another scheme—one of the funniest and most bizarre that anyone could dream up.

The next day the duchess asked Sancho whether he had made a start on the penance he was required to perform for Dulcinea's disenchantment. He said he had, and that he had given himself five lashes the night before.
The duchess asked what he had given them with.
His hand, he said.

“That,” said the duchess, “sounds more like slapping yourself than whipping yourself. I am quite sure the sage Merlin will not be satisfied with such gentleness. Good Sancho will have to get himself a scourge with barbs, or a cat-o'-nine-tails—something that can actually be felt—because learning comes at the price of blood, and the freedom of so great a lady as Dulcinea will not be granted so cheaply or at such a bargain rate. And remember, Sancho, that acts of charity performed in a lukewarm, half-hearted spirit count for nothing and earn no merit.”

To this Sancho answered, “If your ladyship will provide me with a suitable whip or cord, I'll use it on myself—as long as it doesn't hurt too much. Because I should tell you that, peasant though I am, my flesh is more cotton than hemp, and it would hardly make sense for me to ruin myself for somebody else's benefit.”
“Very well, by all means,” said the duchess. “Tomorrow I'll give you a scourge that will suit you perfectly and adapt itself to the tenderness of your flesh as though it were its own sister.”

Then Sancho said, “Your highness should know, dear lady of my soul, that I have written a letter to my wife, Teresa Panza, telling her everything that has happened to me since I left her. I have it right here inside my shirt, and all that's missing is the address. I'd be grateful if your wisdom would read it over, because I believe it's written in the governor style—I mean, the way governors are supposed to write.”
“And who did the dictating?” asked the duchess.
“Who would have dictated it but me, sinner that I am?” said Sancho.
“And did you write it out yourself?” said the duchess.
“Certainly not,” said Sancho, “because I can't read or write—though I can sign my name.”
“Let's have a look at it,” said the duchess, “for I have no doubt you display in it both the quality and the quantity of your wit.”
Sancho pulled an unsealed letter from inside his shirt, and the duchess took it and found that it read as follows:
SANCHO PANZA'S LETTER TO HIS WIFE, TERESA PANZA

If I got a good whipping, at least I rode like a gentleman; if I have landed a fine government, it has cost me a fine flogging. You won't understand this just yet, my Teresa; later on you'll see what it means. Let me tell you, Teresa, that I intend for you to ride in a coach, because that is what matters—any other way of traveling is crawling on all fours. You are a governor's wife now; see to it that nobody speaks ill of you behind your back. I'm sending you a green hunting outfit that my lady the duchess gave me; have it altered into a skirt and bodice for our daughter. Don Quixote, my master, from what I hear people say around here, is a madman with sense in him, an entertaining fool, and I'm not far behind him myself. We have been in the cave of Montesinos, and the sage Merlin has gotten his hands on me for the disenchanting of Dulcinea del Toboso—the one known back home as Aldonza Lorenzo. With three thousand three hundred lashes, minus five, that I'm supposed to give myself, she will end up as thoroughly disenchanted as the mother who bore her. Don't say a word about this to anyone, because if you put your business out in public, some will call it white and others will call it black. In a few days I'll be leaving here for my government, and I'm going to it with a tremendous appetite for making money, since I'm told that all new governors set out with the same appetite. I'll take the pulse of the place and let you know whether you should come and live with me or not. Dapple is well and sends you his warmest regards; I am not leaving him behind even if they carried me off to be Grand Turk. My lady the duchess kisses your hands a thousand times; answer her with two thousand, because, as my master says, nothing costs less or comes cheaper than good manners. God has not seen fit to send me another traveling bag with another hundred crowns in it, like the one the other day; but never mind, my Teresa—the bell-ringer is safe and sound, and everything will come out in the wash of the government. The only thing that really worries me is what people tell me: that once I've had a taste of it I'll gnaw my own hands off craving more; and if that's true, it won't come cheap for me—though, then again, the crippled have a kind of living of their own in the alms they beg; so one way or another you'll end up rich and fortunate. May God grant it to you as he is able, and keep me alive to serve you. From this castle, the 20th of July, 1614.
Your husband, the governor, SANCHO PANZA

When she had finished reading the letter, the duchess said to Sancho, “On two points the worthy governor goes somewhat off course. One is in saying, or implying, that this government has been granted to him in exchange for the lashes he is to give himself, when he knows perfectly well—and cannot deny—that when my lord the duke promised it to him, nobody had so much as dreamed of lashes. The other is that he shows himself here to be very greedy, and I would not want him to be a money-chaser, for ‘greed bursts the bag,’ and a greedy governor delivers justice without governance.”

“That's not how I meant it, señora,” said Sancho, “and if you think the letter doesn't read the way it should, we can just tear it up and write another one—though it may turn out even worse if it's left to my own wits.”
“No, no,” said the duchess, “this one will do nicely, and I want the duke to see it.”

With that they made their way to a garden where they were to dine, and the duchess showed Sancho's letter to the duke, who was thoroughly delighted by it. They ate, and after the table had been cleared and they had entertained themselves for a while with Sancho's rich talk, the mournful sound of a fife and a harsh, jarring drum suddenly reached them. Everyone seemed unsettled by this dull, confused, warlike music—above all Don Quixote, who was so agitated he could hardly stay in his seat; as for Sancho, it goes without saying that fear sent him to his usual refuge, at the duchess's side or in her skirts; and the sound they heard truly was a most dismal and melancholy one. While they were still wondering what it meant, they saw two men coming toward them through the garden, dressed in mourning robes so long and trailing that they dragged along the ground. As they marched they beat two great drums, likewise draped in black, and beside them walked the fife player, as black and somber as the rest. Behind these came a figure of gigantic height, swallowed up rather than dressed in a gown of the deepest black, its train of enormous size. Over the gown, encircling or crossing his body, ran a wide baldric, also black, from which hung a huge scimitar with black scabbard and fittings. His face was covered with a transparent black veil, through which one could make out a very long beard as white as snow. He advanced in time to the drumbeats with great gravity and composure; and in short, his height, his stride, his somber appearance, and his escort were enough to astonish—as indeed they did—everyone who looked at him without knowing who he was. At this measured pace and in this fashion he came forward and knelt before the duke, who, with the others, stood waiting to receive him. The duke, however, absolutely refused to let him speak until he had risen. The prodigious scarecrow obeyed, and once on his feet he lifted the veil from his face and revealed the most enormous, the longest, the whitest, and the thickest beard that human eyes had ever seen up to that moment; then, drawing a grave, resonant voice from the depths of his broad, capacious chest, and fixing his eyes on the duke, he said:

“Most high and mighty señor, my name is Trifaldin of the White Beard. I am squire to the Countess Trifaldi, otherwise known as the Distressed Duenna, on whose behalf I bring a message to your highness: that your magnificence be pleased to grant her leave and permission to come and tell you her trouble, which is one of the strangest and most astonishing that the mind best acquainted with trouble anywhere in the world could ever have conceived. But first she wishes to know whether the valiant and never-defeated knight Don Quixote of La Mancha is in this castle of yours, for she has come in search of him on foot, and without breaking her fast, all the way from the kingdom of Kandy to your realms here—a thing that can and should be taken for a miracle, or else attributed to enchantment. She is at this very moment at the gate of this fortress or pleasure-house, and waits only for your permission to enter. I have spoken.” At this he coughed, smoothed his beard down with both hands, and stood very calmly awaiting the duke's reply, which ran as follows: “Many days ago, worthy squire Trifaldin of the White Beard, we heard of the misfortune of my lady the Countess Trifaldi, whom the enchanters have caused to be called the Distressed Duenna. Tell her to enter, O stupendous squire, and tell her that the valiant knight Don Quixote of La Mancha is here, and that from his generous nature she may confidently promise herself every protection and assistance. You may add that if my own help should be needed, it will not be refused, for I am obliged to give it by my rank as a knight, which carries with it the protection of women of every kind—above all widowed, wronged, and distressed ladies, as her ladyship appears to be.”

Hearing this, Trifaldin dropped to one knee, and signaling to the fifer and the drummers to strike up, he turned and marched out of the garden to the same music and at the same pace as when he had entered, leaving everyone amazed at his bearing and solemnity. Turning to Don Quixote, the duke said, “In the end, renowned knight, the fogs of malice and ignorance cannot hide or dim the light of valor and virtue. I say this because your excellence has been barely six days in this castle, and already the unhappy and the afflicted come seeking you from distant and far-off lands—not in coaches or on dromedaries, but on foot and fasting—confident that in that mighty arm of yours they will find the cure for their sorrows and troubles; and all thanks to your great deeds, which are talked of across the whole known earth.”

“I wish, señor duke,” Don Quixote replied, “that the blessed churchman who showed such ill will and bitter spite toward knights-errant at table the other day were here right now, to see with his own eyes whether knights of that kind are needed in the world. He would at least learn from experience that those who suffer any extraordinary affliction or sorrow, in desperate circumstances and uncommon misfortunes, do not go looking for a remedy in the houses of lawyers or village sacristans, nor to the knight who has never ventured beyond the limits of his own town, nor to the idle courtier who would rather hunt for gossip to repeat and pass along than strive to perform deeds and exploits for others to recount and record. Relief in distress, help in time of need, protection for maidens, comfort for widows—these are found in no kind of person better than in knights-errant; and I give unending thanks to heaven that I am one, and I count any misfortune or hardship that may come my way in pursuing so honorable a calling as suffering well spent. Let this duenna come and ask whatever she pleases, for I will deliver her remedy through the strength of my arm and the fearless resolve of my courageous heart.”
